projects.title: MCU Data Logger
projects.intro: A compact ATmega328P data-logging board, now in its second revision. Rev A proved the core layout with zero KiCad errors; Rev B redesigns it for battery operation with a protected 3.3 V supply, a backed-up DS3231 RTC that can wake the MCU, and a full set of programming and expansion connectors.
projects.status: Rev B · schematic + PCB complete · 0 DRC errors
projects.caption: Rev A · KiCad 3D render of the final routed board

sections.title: The challenge
sections.text: Develop a compact microcontroller board with nonvolatile storage, timekeeping, accessible interfaces, and programming connections for future data-logging firmware.

sections.title: Engineering work
sections.text: ATmega328P-AUR in TQFP-32, two 24LC1025 I²C EEPROMs, a DS1337 RTC, and separate 16 MHz and 32.768 kHz crystals. UART, I²C, GPIO, and a 2×3 ISP header expose the development interfaces in an approximately 52.1 × 34.9 mm two-layer board.

sections.title: Verification
sections.text: KiCad reports zero DRC violations, zero unconnected pads, zero footprint/parity errors, and zero schematic ERC errors or warnings. The final board includes a filled B.Cu ground zone, explicit manufacturing rules, and wider power traces where clearance permits.

sections.title: Design completion & next steps
sections.text: Gerber and drill files are generated from the verified board. This is a hardware CAD and fabrication package; firmware development, board assembly, power-up checks, and physical performance testing remain bring-up work.

sections.title: Rev B redesign
sections.text: A review of Rev A found a battery wired straight onto the supply, a 16 MHz clock running out of spec at low voltage, an RTC alarm that could not reach the MCU, no clock backup, and too little decoupling. Rev B fixes each one: reverse-polarity protection (DMG2305UX) and Schottky power-OR into an MCP1700 1.6 µA LDO, 3.3 V operation with an 8 MHz crystal, a DS3231 TCXO RTC with CR2032 backup and its alarm on INT0, 100 nF at every supply pin, a battery-voltage divider on ADC7, plus FTDI auto-reset, ISP, Qwiic and broken-out analog inputs. Parts were checked on DigiKey and placed from the EasyEDA/LCSC library with matching footprints.

sections.title: Rev B layout
sections.text: 73.7 × 45.7 mm, two layers, ground pours on both sides and 64 vias. EasyEDA Pro reports 0 schematic and 0 PCB DRC errors. Routing was auto-generated and is due a manual pass before ordering; mounting holes and silkscreen clean-up are the remaining Rev B tasks.

projects.title: Photodiode TIA & Wireless Optical Sensor
projects.intro: An end-to-end light-to-data chain: a selectable-gain photodiode transimpedance front end, simulated in LTspice and laid out in KiCad, feeding timer-driven ESP32 acquisition, a live Flutter dashboard and Python FFT analysis.
projects.status: Analog design + PCB complete · ESP32 stream live at 1 kS/s
projects.caption: Rev A top view rendered from the exported Gerber and drill files.
projects.imageAlt: Gerber-derived top view of the 60 by 45 mm photodiode TIA PCB, showing gain links, routing, pads and the external ESP32 connector.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Convert photodiode current into a usable voltage, then carry the samples through embedded acquisition, wireless telemetry, and host-side analysis. The BPW34 is the provisional reference detector; the ESP32 DevKit connects through a cable header rather than being fitted to the analog PCB.

sections.title: Analog front end
sections.text: OPA2320 amplifiers provide the transimpedance stage, buffered 1.65 V reference, and filter followers. Three paired feedback selections—10 kΩ / 1 nF, 100 kΩ / 100 pF, and 1 MΩ / 10 pF—set the gain and compensation. A TPS7A2033PDBVR regulator supplies the analog rail; a series resistor and BAT54S clamp protect the ADC input.

sections.title: Simulation & validation
sections.text: SIMULATED in LTspice using the TI OPAx320 model: approximately 15.9 kHz TIA bandwidth and 309.5 Hz conditioned-system bandwidth. Nominal phase margins are 79.4°, 85.5°, and 90.4° across the selected gains. The analog design gate passed; these are model results, not hardware measurements.

sections.title: PCB design
sections.text: The 60 × 45 mm two-layer layout keeps the photodiode/TIA input path short, clusters the feedback pairs, and excludes copper pour around sensitive summing and feedback nodes. Repository verification records clean ERC, DRC, connectivity, and schematic/PCB parity, plus a complete BOM and Gerber/drill package for bare-board prototype fabrication.

sections.title: Firmware
sections.text: ESP32 ADC1 / GPIO34 acquisition is driven by a hardware timer and buffered separately from WebSocket telemetry. Firmware is running on the ESP32 Dev Module. The current live-demo default is 1 kS/s: a fresh 10-second Wi-Fi capture delivered 9,984 samples with no new device drops or missing packet sequences. The 4 kS/s design target still loses samples in the tested setup, so its transport path needs further work.

sections.title: Flutter dashboard
sections.text: The Flutter web dashboard displays the live ADC waveform, raw counts, calibrated pin millivolts, sample rate and packet-health counters. It reconnects after ESP32 resets and distinguishes device data from an optional simulated demo. Because the photodiode/TIA board is not assembled, the recorded GPIO34 input is floating; the changing readings are not optical measurements.

sections.title: Python analysis
sections.text: Host tools provide waveform viewing, CSV recording, FFT, dark/no-signal noise analysis, and gain/frequency-response workflows. Seven offline tests and a synthetic capture-to-FFT smoke check are recorded as passing on September 29, 2026. Synthetic data validates software behavior; it is not measured optical performance.

sections.title: Phase-sensitive sensing research
sections.text: An in-progress research track adds timestamp-aware lock-in estimation and a seeded synthetic comparison against raw-range and known-frequency FFT methods. With GPIO34 open, a 15-second test sent 14,848 samples to each of three simultaneous Python receivers at 1 kS/s, with no measured device drops or sequence gaps. At 4 kS/s, a single-receiver 12-second test delivered 42,240 samples and reported 4,096 new drops. These short local-network captures establish a demo operating point and an unresolved throughput limit; they are not optical detection results.

sections.title: Project status
sections.text: DESIGN / SIMULATION / PCB / SOFTWARE COMPLETE. The ESP32 Dev Module and Flutter stream have been demonstrated with an unconnected ADC input. Revision A remains unmanufactured. Analog hardware characterization has not yet been performed; assembly, calibration, and bench validation remain the next steps.

decisions.title: Gain without losing stability
decisions.problem: Different photocurrent ranges require different transimpedance gains.
decisions.decision: Select paired RF / CF values: 10 kΩ / 1 nF, 100 kΩ / 100 pF, or 1 MΩ / 10 pF.
decisions.evidence: LTspice sweeps show 79.4°, 85.5° and 90.4° phase margin across the three gains (TI OPAx320 model).

decisions.title: Separate acquisition from transport
decisions.problem: Wireless transport must not own the sampling schedule.
decisions.decision: Use a hardware timer to wake acquisition, with buffering separate from WebSocket telemetry.
decisions.evidence: Live 10-second single-receiver and 15-second three-receiver captures at 1 kS/s had no new drops or sequence gaps. A 4 kS/s capture showed drops; the stream-health report records the conditions and limits.

Three paired RF / CF networks and output-side links select one compensated gain.
Two buffered low-pass sections condition the signal before the ADC.
The series resistor and BAT54S clamp limit the ADC input excursions.

pcb: Detector input and U1 sit close together, with sensitive summing-node copper kept compact.
Feedback pairs run beside U1, below the three gain-selection links.
U1 includes the reference buffer; the analog regulator is near the upper-right supply entrance.
The conditioned output reaches the ADC link jumper before the ESP32 header.

projects.title: Photoacoustic Tomography Acquisition System
projects.intro: Undergraduate research at Iowa State University: building the receive and acquisition hardware for pulsed-LED photoacoustic tomography — an eight-channel VCA8500 variable-gain receive board, now routed at revision v2, feeding STM32H7 timer/DMA sampling.
projects.caption: Planned acquisition architecture under development

sections.title: Research context
sections.text: Developing a microcontroller-based acquisition platform for pulsed-LED photoacoustic tomography at Iowa State University, working with Prof. Manojit Pramanik.

sections.title: My focus
sections.text: Timer-triggered ADC sampling, DMA-to-RAM buffering, memory organization, and peripheral integration. The design work explores how timing and data movement constrain an embedded acquisition pipeline.

sections.title: VCA8500 analog front end
sections.text: Designed an eight-channel VCA8500 receive board in KiCad, starting from a datasheet-based reference schematic. The routed v2 layout places the VCA8500 at the centre with eight AC-coupled inputs (J1–J8) on the left and right edges, eight differential output channels (J9–J16) along the bottom, per-channel test points, a control header for reset, serial programming, power-down and VCNTL, separate +5 V / +3.3 V supply entry, and a ground pour around the package.

sections.title: VCA8500 simulation evidence
sections.text: Swept the TI single-channel model in LTspice with a 5 MHz, 20 µVpp input while varying VCNTL from 0 to 1.2 V: modeled OUT+ amplitude rose from 7.4 µVpp to 1.32 mVpp, about 45 dB of control range. These are simulation results, not measured receive-chain performance.

sections.title: System direction
sections.text: The development plan connects STM32H7 acquisition to a planned ESP32 gateway and host interface. MCU selection and end-to-end integration remain development decisions.

sections.title: Current evidence
sections.text: Ongoing research. The v2 board layout and the gain-control simulation are complete; fabrication, bring-up and end-to-end hardware validation are next.

projects.title: Power-System Monitoring Interfaces
projects.intro: Built ESP32 display and Flutter interface prototypes for power-system telemetry, combining touch controls, rolling plots, BLE, and WebSocket communication.
projects.caption: Bench prototype photographed at IIT Hyderabad, and the PPS Monitor Flutter app

sections.title: The challenge
sections.text: Make power-system information usable on small embedded screens and mobile devices: clear values, responsive graphs, and accessible controls across different communication paths.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: Built ESP32 TFT interfaces with selective redraw, debounced buttons, scrolling graph buffers, and touch calibration. Developed Flutter views for telemetry, graphing, and command interactions.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.text: The report describes W5500 Ethernet, Bluetooth Classic, BLE, and later Wi-Fi variants. The public Flutter code implements BLE discovery, WebSocket transport, six-field telemetry parsing, rolling plots, and control messages.

sections.title: Evidence & limits
sections.text: The public ESP32 firmware streams simulated readings and logs received commands, demonstrating the communication and interface layers end to end. A potentiometer served as the live analog input on the touchscreen prototype.

projects.title: Four-Node ESP32 Ethernet Telemetry
projects.intro: Four ESP32 boards with W5500 Ethernet each stream to their own panel of a Flutter dashboard over independent WebSocket connections, with live status and per-device CSV recording.
projects.status: IIT Hyderabad · demonstrated on four boards
projects.caption: Report photographs of the four-panel Flutter dashboard. Each graph is an independent ESP32/W5500 connection.

sections.title: Four independent data streams
sections.text: Built a Flutter visualizer supporting four ESP32 boards with W5500 Ethernet modules. Each board runs its own WebSocket server on port 81 and streams mathematically generated sine-wave data to a separate graph.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: Maintained four independent WebSocketChannel instances with separate listeners, editable device IPs, connection status, and a CustomPainter graph per ESP32. Added per-device recording and clipboard-based CSV export. Generated waveforms exercise communication and visualization; they are not measured sensor signals.

sections.title: Another four-board experiment
sections.text: The report also documents four ESP32 boards and four W5500 modules arranged as three senders and one receiver. Sender IDs determine priority, with ESP1 ranked above ESP2 and ESP3.

sections.title: Report evidence
sections.text: The report documents the four-channel dashboard and records successful sender connections and priority-based acceptance/rejection in the separate messaging experiment. It does not establish hardware clock synchronization, fault-tolerant failover, or a validated latency benchmark.
